content.content: # Managed certificate renewal in AWS Certificate Manager ACM provides managed renewal for your Amazon-issued SSL/TLS certificates. This means that ACM will either renew your certificates automatically (if you are using DNS validation), or it will send you email notices when expiration is approaching. These services are provided for both public and private ACM certificates. A certificate is eligible for automatic renewal subject to the following considerations: + ELIGIBLE if associated with another AWS service, such as Elastic Load Balancing or CloudFront. + ELIGIBLE if exported since being issued or last renewed. + ELIGIBLE if it is a private certificate issued by calling the ACM [RequestCertificate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/APIReference/API_RequestCertificate.html) API *and* then exported or associated with another AWS service. + ELIGIBLE if it is a private certificate issued through the [management console](gs-acm-request-private.md) *and* then exported or associated with another AWS service. + NOT ELIGIBLE if it is a private certificate issued by calling the AWS Private CA [IssueCertificate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/privateca/latest/APIReference/API_IssueCertificate.html) API. + NOT ELIGIBLE if [imported](import-certificate.md). + NOT ELIGIBLE if already expired. **Note** Certificates issued through ACME certificate automation are not eligible for ACM managed renewal. Renewal of ACME certificates is managed by the ACME client. For more information, see [Issuing certificates through ACME](acm-acme-issuance.md). Additionally, the following [Punycode](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3492) requirements relating to [Internationalized Domain Names](https://www.icann.org/resources/pages/idn-2012-02-25-en) must be fulfilled: 1. Domain names beginning with the pattern "--" must match "xn--". 1. Domain names beginning with "xn--" must also be valid Internationalized Domain Names. **Punycode examples** | Domain Name | Fulfills \#1 | Fulfills \#2 | Allowed | Note | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | example.com | n/a | n/a | ✓ | Does not start with "--" | | a--example.com | n/a | n/a | ✓ | Does not start with "--" | | abc--example.com | n/a | n/a | ✓ | Does not start with "--" | | xn--xyz.com | Yes | Yes | ✓ | Valid Internationalized Domain Name (resolves to 简.com) | | xn--example.com | Yes | No | ✗ | Not a valid Internationalized Domain Name | | ab--example.com | No | No | ✗ | Must start with "xn--" | When ACM renews a certificate, the certificate's Amazon Resource Name (ARN) remains the same. Also, ACM certificates are [regional resources](acm-overview.md#acm-regions). If you have certificates for the same domain name in multiple AWS Regions, each of these certificates must be renewed independently. **Topics** + [Renew ACM public certificates](renew-publicly-trusted.md) + [Private certificate renewal in AWS Certificate Manager](renew-private-cert.md) + [Check a certificate's renewal status](check-certificate-renewal-status.md)

content.content:
# Certbot Renewal Automation Details

## (1) How Certbot Automates Renewal

Certbot uses scheduled tasks to run renewals automatically:

> "Most Certbot installations come with automatic renewals preconfigured. This is done by means of a scheduled task which runs `certbot renew` periodically."

For Linux/BSD systems, this typically involves a cron job:

> "0 0,12 * * * root sleep $SLEEPTIME && certbot renew -q"

This command runs renewal checks twice daily (at midnight and noon).

## (2) Renewal Eligibility Criteria

Certbot determines renewal readiness based on certificate lifetime:

> "As of Certbot 4.0.0, a certificate is considered ready for renewal when less than 1/3rd of its lifetime remains. For certificates with a lifetime of 10 days or less, that threshold is 1/2 of the lifetime."

## (3) Deploy Hook Mechanism

The deploy hook allows administrators to execute commands after successful renewal:

> "When Certbot detects that a certificate is due for renewal, `--pre-hook` and `--post-hook` hooks run before and after each attempt to renew it. If you want your hook to run only after a successful renewal, use `--deploy-hook`"

Example usage: `certbot renew --deploy-hook /path/to/deploy-hook-script`

This enables automatic web server reloads following successful certificate updates.

"Up to 5 authorization failures per identifier can be incurred by one account every hour."

Once exceeded, this prevents "any new orders for the same identifier, by the same account until the limit resets."

"Up to 1,152 consecutive authorization failures per identifier can be incurred by one account." Exceeding this causes the account to be "prevented from requesting new certificates for that identifier."

"Up to 5 certificates can be issued per exact same set of identifiers every 7 days." This applies globally across all accounts.

101	**(b) Speculative chain** — Criterion 5. A chain is explicitly marked speculative and the
102	analysis states the claim it supports is not load-bearing; the mark plus that statement is
103	the satisfying evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM.
104	
105	**(c) Absent-fails derivation** — Criterion 5. A chain establishes that a conclusion does not
106	follow from an assumption shown to be false; the named false assumption is the satisfying
107	evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM.
108	
109	An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one names it in the relevant
110	verdict block and cites the required evidence; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the
111	analysis's behalf.

115	## Scoring Model
116	
117	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
118	(highest to lowest):
119	
120	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
121	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
122	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
123	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
124	
125	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
126	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
127	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
128	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
129	
130	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
131	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
132	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
133	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
134	
135	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
136	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
137	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
138	
139	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
140	
141	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised before
142	conclusions are presented, regardless of how all other criteria score.
143	
144	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
145	it must be revised before conclusions are presented. One criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated
146	(one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic quality problem); two or more at
147	Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the gate alone cannot catch, because
148	no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level.
149	
150	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
151	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
152	
153	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
154	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
155	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
156	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
157	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
158	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
159	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
160	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
161	content.
162	
163	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
164	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
165	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
166	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
167	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
168	high-stakes conclusion.")

217	### Criterion 1: Identify Essence
218	
219	Scores the **Essence Statement** — the single sentence naming the core problem followed by
220	a short list of success criteria — in the Problem Essence section (output section 1).
221	
222	- **Rigorous** — the Essence Statement is a single sentence that names the core question or
223	  decision (not a symptom, not the triggering event, not a restatement of the user's prompt);
224	  each success criterion contains a pass/fail structural test — a verb + subject + outcome
225	  triplet where the outcome is a property of the Conclusion section — so that a reviewer
226	  applies each criterion by scanning the Conclusion section without analyst interpretation;
227	  the statement is specific enough that it appears nowhere in an analysis of a different but
228	  related problem without modification (it names a property unique to this problem, not a
229	  generic template phrase).
230	  If this section uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`), the
231	  stated reason is specific to this analysis's problem — it names a property of the problem
232	  that makes an Essence Statement unnecessary or redundant, and that reason appears in no
233	  other analysis without alteration.
234	
235	- **Sound** — the Essence Statement exists and names a question, but the success criteria are
236	  vague or stated in terms that cannot be verified against the conclusion without further
237	  clarification (e.g., "the solution should be good," "the approach should be appropriate").
238	
239	- **Hand-wavy** — the Essence Statement exists but names a symptom, a triggering event, or a
240	  restatement of the user's prompt rather than the underlying question; OR the success criteria
241	  are absent while the Essence Statement itself is present; OR the section uses the honest-depth
242	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
243	  "no essence was needed").
244	
245	- **Absent** — no Essence Statement is present (the Problem Essence section is empty, contains
246	  only a restatement of the original prompt with no analytical distillation, or the section
247	  heading appears with nothing below it).
248	  This verdict routes back to Phase 1 to re-frame the Essence Statement — or, when the cause is an input that was never supplied, to re-opening input under the Input Contract — rather than an in-place rewrite of output section 1; the route is bounded by the same rule described under `SKILL.md`'s "Before presenting conclusions" section.

253	Verdict, Verification — in the Assumptions Table section (output section 2). Folds in:
254	four-type classification quality and unverified-flag discipline (D-07).
255	
256	- **Rigorous** — every row in the Assumptions Table has a Type value drawn from exactly the
257	  four-type scheme (physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief); the

268	  this scan was exhaustive over named derivation chain steps, not an open-ended survey of the

272	  the Verification cell reads "unclear" or "unsure" without specifics, OR the Treatment
273	  cell records a treatment that does not match the prescribed treatment for the row's Type,
274	  OR one assumption that is used in a chain despite being unverified lacks the
275	  "unverified — flagged" notation.
276	
277	- **Hand-wavy** — the table exists but uses Type values outside the four-type scheme (e.g.,
278	  "general assumption," "business constraint," freeform labels); OR multiple rows have empty
279	  Verdict or Verification cells; OR every assumption is labelled Accept with no challenge
280	  attempted and no evidence cited for any verdict.
281	
282	- **Absent** — no Assumptions Table is present; OR the table exists but every row's Type
283	  cell is empty, freeform (no mapping to the four-type scheme), or missing — making the

286	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
287	
288	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
289	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
290	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
291	
292	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
293	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
294	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
295	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
296	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
297	
298	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
299	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
300	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
301	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
302	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
303	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
304	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
305	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
306	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
307	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
308	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
309	
310	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
311	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
312	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
313	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
314	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
315	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
316	
317	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
318	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
319	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
320	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
321	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
322	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
323	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
324	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
325	
326	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
327	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
328	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
329	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
330	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
331	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
332	
333	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
334	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
335	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
336	
337	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
338	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
339	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
340	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
341	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
342	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
343	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
344	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
345	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
346	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
347	
348	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
349	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
350	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
351	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
352	
353	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
354	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
355	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
356	  section is absent or empty.

358	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
359	
360	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
361	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
362	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
363	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, or a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
364	dead-end honesty
365	and the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), and escape-valve policing for Abandoned
366	Reasoning (D-03). The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
367	
368	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
369	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
370	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
371	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
372	  section either documents
373	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
374	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
375	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
376	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
377	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
378	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
379	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
380	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token.
381	
382	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
383	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
384	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR

399	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that

405	
406	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
407	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in

414	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).

484	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
485	
486	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the three lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
487	
488	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
489	
490	---
491	
492	## Usage Note
493	
494	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
495	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
496	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
497	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
498	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
499	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
500	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
501	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

2	
3	# First Principles Analysis Output Template
4	
5	> **Note:** This is the full annotated template with complete section guidance, type
6	> definitions, and prescriptions. A condensed skeleton showing just the required section
7	> names and chain format lives resident in the agent body (`SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface) for quick reference. Come here
8	> for the complete instructions when authoring or reviewing an analysis.
9	
10	## How to Use This Template
11	
12	This template is a **strict-shape document**. All six sections must be present in the fixed order below. No section may be omitted.
13	
14	If a section has no genuine content for a given analysis — because the problem is simple, the domain has no relevant dead ends, or the section truly does not apply — mark it with the honest-depth escape valve:
15	
16	> `Nothing material here — [reason explaining why this section has no content for this particular analysis and that the omission is justified, not lazy]`
17	
18	The section heading must still appear. The escape valve exists to prevent box-ticking fabrication: it is always better to write `Nothing material here — [reason]` than to fill a section with words that say nothing.
19	
20	**Section order (fixed):**
21	1. Problem Essence
22	2. Assumptions Table
23	3. Ground Truths
24	4. Derivation Chains
25	5. Abandoned Reasoning
26	6. Conclusion
27	
28	---
29	
30	## 1. Problem Essence
31	
32	State the core problem in a single sentence — not the symptoms, not the solution space, but the irreducible question the analysis must answer.
33	
34	**Core problem:** [One sentence. Strip away implementation details and surface the underlying question.]
35	
36	**Success criteria:** [Measurable, observable outcomes that would confirm the problem is solved. A skeptic must be able to verify these without asking for further clarification.]
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 2. Assumptions Table
41	
42	List every assumption — explicit and implicit — that the analysis rests on. Classify each by type and apply the prescribed treatment. An assumption omitted from this table is an assumption that will propagate unchallenged through every later step.
43	
44	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
45	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
46	| [Assumption text] | [physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief] | [prescribed action per type — see below] | [Accept / Challenge / Discard] — [justification/reason] | [source, or "unverified — flagged" if used in a chain per D-07] |
47	
48	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
49	
50	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
51	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
52	
53	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
54	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
55	
56	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
57	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
58	
59	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
60	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
61	
62	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
63	
64	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
65	
66	### Verdict Vocabulary
67	
68	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
69	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning:
70	
71	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
72	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
73	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
74	
75	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
76	
77	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
78	
79	```text
80	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
81	```
82	
83	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
84	
85	```text
86	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
87	```
88	
89	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## 3. Ground Truths
94	
95	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
96	
97	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
98	
99	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
100	
101	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
102	
103	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
104	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
105	
106	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
107	
108	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
109	
110	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
111	
112	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
113	
114	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
115	
116	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
117	
118	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a HIGH-confidence chain, name its read-at-source location. Write the list, not a number:
119	
120	```text
121	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
122	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
123	```
124	
125	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
126	
127	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## 4. Derivation Chains
132	
133	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
134	
135	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
136	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
137	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
138	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
139	
140	**Chain format:**
141	
142	```text
143	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
144	```
145	
146	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
147	
148	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
149	
150	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
151	
152	```text
153	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
154	→ [intermediate claim]
155	→ [further intermediate]
156	→ [conclusion]
157	```
158	
159	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
160	
161	```text
162	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
163	→ [intermediate claim]
164	→ [conclusion]
165	```
166	
167	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
168	
169	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
170	
171	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
172	
173	```text
174	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
175	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
176	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
177	```
178	
179	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
180	
181	```text
182	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
183	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
184	  once idle-time billing is included
185	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
186	```
187	
188	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
189	
190	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
191	
192	```text
193	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
194	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
195	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
196	```
197	
198	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
199	
200	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
201	
202	```text
203	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
204	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
205	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
206	```
207	
208	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
209	
210	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
211	
212	```text
213	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
214	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
215	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
216	```
217	
218	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
219	
220	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
221	
222	```text
223	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
224	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
225	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
226	```
227	
228	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
229	
230	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
231	
232	```text
233	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
234	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
235	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
236	```
237	
238	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
239	
240	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
241	
242	```text
243	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
244	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
245	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
246	```
247	
248	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
249	
250	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
251	
252	```text
253	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
254	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
255	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
256	```
257	
258	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
259	
260	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
261	
262	```text
263	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
264	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
265	→ the second reading is the binding one
266	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
267	```
268	
269	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
270	
271	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
272	
273	```text
274	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
275	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
276	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
277	```
278	
279	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
280	
281	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
282	
283	```text
284	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
285	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
286	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
287	```
288	
289	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
290	
291	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
292	
293	```text
294	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
295	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
296	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
297	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
298	```
299	
300	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
301	
302	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
303	
304	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
305	
306	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
307	
308	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
309	
310	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
311	
312	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
313	
314	```text
315	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
316	```
317	
318	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
319	
320	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
321	
322	```text
323	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
324	```
325	
326	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
327	
328	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
329	
330	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
331	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
332	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
333	
334	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
335	[If MEDIUM or LOW: state which GT-N? input caused the downgrade and what would need to be verified to raise confidence.]
336	
337	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state what verification would raise confidence to HIGH. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth.
338	
339	---
340	
341	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
342	
343	Record every reasoning path that was explored and discarded. This section is required in every analysis. Dead ends are not failures — they are part of the reasoning record and save future analysts from re-exploring paths that have already been ruled out.
344	
345	### Dead End: [Name of discarded path]
346	
347	**What was tried:** [Brief description of the reasoning path that was pursued.]
348	
349	**Why abandoned:** [The specific failure — assumption false, contradicts a ground truth, assumption classification too weak to anchor the chain, conclusion circular, intermediate could not be established, etc. Be precise: "we ran out of time" is not a valid abandonment reason.]
350	
351	**What it ruled out:** [What this dead end saves the reader from re-exploring. A well-documented dead end is as valuable as a live conclusion.]
352	
353	If no reasoning was abandoned, write:
354	
355	`Nothing material here — all reasoning paths pursued led to the conclusion above. [Optional: describe the problem's constraint space that made alternative paths infeasible.]`
356	
357	The escape valve still satisfies D-03. Do not omit the heading.
358	
359	---
360	
361	## 6. Conclusion
362	
363	Summarize the analysis result. The Conclusion section synthesizes what the Derivation Chains established — it does not introduce new claims or reasoning.
364	
365	**Recommended approach:** [Description of the recommended course of action, decision, or design choice.]
366	
367	**Key insight:** [The non-obvious finding the first-principles analysis revealed — what reasoning by analogy or convention would have missed.]
368	
369	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** [What is being accepted, deprioritized, or deferred as a result of this recommendation. No recommendation is free of trade-offs.]
370	
371	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
372	
373	If Confidence is MEDIUM or LOW: name the specific `GT-N?` inputs from the Derivation Chains that caused the downgrade and state what verification would raise confidence to HIGH. A MEDIUM or LOW conclusion without this explanation does not satisfy D-07.
374	
375	**Claim inventory.** A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the three lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
376	
377	**Citation form.** Every Conclusion-section claim either names the chain that established it inline — `(chain C1)` — or is discharged by a §6→§4 closure ledger row that quotes the claim and names its chain. A claim doing neither is cut, not softened. Ledger discharge requires the structural row form the closure-ledger example below shows — a list marker, then the quoted claim, then an arrow, then the chain id — and a prose sentence that merely quotes something and names a chain is not a ledger row. This is detected only when the row sits inside section 6: the ledger emitted as process output before the analysis is not visible to the check, and inline citation is therefore the mechanically checkable form.
378	
379	**Conforming — inline chain citation:**
380	
381	```text
382	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate (chain C1).
383	```
384	
385	**Conforming — closure-ledger row:**
386	
387	```text
388	- "Move sustained workloads to Fargate" → chain C1 ✓
389	```
390	
391	**Non-conforming — a claim naming no chain and quoted by no ledger row:**
392	
393	```text
394	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate.
395	```
396	
397	Both forms are accepted because both discharge the same obligation: the ledger is process output emitted before the analysis (see the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions"), not a seventh output section, and the chain IDs cited are the `C1`/`C2` IDs assigned by §4's chain-numbering convention.
398	
399	**Caveats.** A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
400	
401	**Not a claim — a bold lead-in alone on its line, carrying no citation:**
402	
403	```text
404	**Recommended approach — three steps, in this order:**
405	```
406	
407	This is the hinge of "detectable from the emission alone" — an author can dodge extraction by putting the lead-in on its own line, and the claim obligation then falls to the numbered items beneath it.
408	
409	**A claim — the same lead-in carrying its assertion on the same line:**
410	
411	```text
412	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate before evaluating Lambda (chain C1).
413	```
414	
415	Nothing follows the closing `**` in the block above and something does here, which is the whole difference.
416	
417	**A claim — the lead-in alone on its line, but carrying its own citation:**
418	
419	```text
420	**Recommended approach, established in chain C1:**
421	```
422	
423	The section-intro-label exclusion is conditional on carrying no citation; naming the chain inside the label keeps it a claim.
424	
425	**Not matched at all — a bold span whose colon sits inside it:**
426	
427	```text
428	**Overall confidence: HIGH.**
429	```
430	
431	The extractor requires the colon to close the bold span, so this line is not a claim and not a non-claim — it is never looked at.
432	
433	**A claim — the same statement with the colon closing the bold span:**
434	
435	```text
436	**Overall confidence:** HIGH — seven of eight chains rest on figures read at source (chain C1).
437	```
438	
439	One character moved, and the statement enters the inventory.
440	
441	**Not a claim — a short list item with no sentence-ending punctuation:**
442	
443	```text
444	- Measure duty cycle first
445	```
446	
447	Twenty-four characters and no terminal punctuation, so it falls under the assertiveness floor.
448	
449	**A claim — a short list item closing its own sentence:**
450	
451	```text
452	- Size the Savings Plan after cleanup.
453	```
454	
455	Also under forty characters, so the terminal punctuation is the only thing carrying it over the floor. The two items above are worded differently only so each block is uniquely locatable by the fixture-extraction guard — a true one-character minimal pair would make one block's text a literal prefix of the other's, which no substring needle can discriminate (the `R-HEAD-PERIOD-*` lesson) — and a later control proves the axis is punctuation by re-scoring each block with its punctuation toggled.
456	
457	**Conformant but still untraced — a caveat carrying the flagged-assumption marker:**
458	
459	```text
460	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower — no chain — flagged assumption only.
461	```
462	
463	The marker satisfies the Caveats rule above and the claim still scores untraced; that is honesty-not-score, not a defect, and it is why the extractor is not taught to recognise the marker.
464	
465	**Conformant and traced — the same caveat citing the chain it qualifies:**
466	
467	```text
468	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower (chain C5).
469	```
470	
471	Naming C5 discharges the claim; the marker discloses it. The two rewrites land on different Criterion 6 bands, and that band is assigned by a model — no gate in this tree checks it.
